title: Module Overview: d-Dimensional EST Diophantine Approximation
content: This module opens with the derivation sketch for the d-dimensional Erdős–Szüsz–Turán formula. The key steps: (1) in the EST regime, approximation boxes for different denominators are disjoint; (2) each primitive vector p with denominator q contributes (2A/q^{1+1/d})^d volume; (3) summing over q ∈ [N,cN] gives S_d ≈ (2A)^d · Σ J_d(q)/q^{d+1}; (4) the Jordan-Mertens theorem evaluates this sum as log(c)/ζ(d+1). The docstring explicitly records 0 sorries and 9 axioms, and notes the EST regime condition A < 1/(2(d+1)).
mathContext: The d-dimensional approximation set: $S_d(N,A,c) \approx (2A)^d \sum_{q=N}^{cN} \frac{J_d(q)}{q^{d+1}}$ where $J_d(q) = \#\{p \in \mathbb{Z}^d_q : \gcd(p,q)=1\}$ is Jordan's $d$-th totient. By Jordan-Mertens: $\sum_{q=N}^{cN} J_d(q)/q^{d+1} \to \log(c)/\zeta(d+1)$, giving $\lim S_d = (2A)^d \log(c)/\zeta(d+1)$.

title: zetaAtSucc: Riemann Zeta Values at Positive Integers
content: The `zetaAtSucc d` definition extracts the real part of ζ(d+1) from Lean's complex Riemann zeta function (`riemannZeta`). Four axioms capture the key analytic properties: positivity, the Basel problem ζ(2)=π²/6, the trivial lower bound ζ(d+1)≥1, and the limit ζ(d+1)→1 as d→∞. These axioms are all provable in principle using Mathlib's analytic number theory, but require more advanced tools than are conveniently available. The Basel problem axiom is the critical one: it ties the d=1 formula to the classical EST result 12A·log(c)/π².
mathContext: The Riemann zeta function $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-s}$ for $\text{Re}(s) > 1$. Key values: $\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$ (Basel problem, Euler 1734), $\zeta(3) \approx 1.202$ (Apéry's constant, irrational by Apéry 1979), $\zeta(4) = \pi^4/90$, $\zeta(2k) = (2\pi)^{2k}|B_{2k}|/(2(2k)!)$ (Bernoulli numbers). $\zeta(s) \to 1$ as $s \to \infty$.

title: jordanTotient: d-Dimensional Generalization of Euler's φ
content: Jordan's totient J_d(q) counts the number of d-tuples of integers in {0,...,q-1}^d that are 'primitive' modulo q (i.e., coprime to q in some coordinate). The Lean definition uses `Nat.card` of a subtype, though the condition in the subtype is slightly informal (the `primeFactors.prod` expression). Two axioms state: J_1 = Euler's φ (the d=1 case), and J_d(q) ≤ q^d (the trivial upper bound). The multiplicative formula J_d(q) = q^d ∏_{p|q}(1-p^{-d}) is implicit but not stated as an axiom here.
mathContext: Jordan's $d$-th totient: $J_d(q) = q^d \prod_{p \text{ prime}, p|q}\left(1 - p^{-d}\right)$. Special cases: $J_1(q) = \varphi(q)$ (Euler's totient), $J_2(q) = q^2 \prod_{p|q}(1-p^{-2})$. The Dirichlet series: $\sum_{q=1}^\infty J_d(q)/q^s = \zeta(s)/\zeta(s+d)$ for $\text{Re}(s) > d+1$. Crucial: at $s = d+1$, this gives $\sum J_d(q)/q^{d+1} = \zeta(d+1)/\zeta(2d+1)$.

title: isApproximable_d and approximationSet_d: The d-Dimensional Approximation Condition
content: The `isApproximable_d` predicate captures simultaneous Diophantine approximation: α ∈ [0,1]^d is (A,d,q)-approximable if there exists a primitive integer vector p such that each coordinate |α_i - p_i/q| < A/q^{1+1/d}. The Chebyshev distance (max norm) is used, consistent with the original EST framework. The `approximationSet_d` collects all such α with denominators in [N,cN]. The `S_d` measure is then the Lebesgue measure of this set in [0,1]^d (using the product measure pi). The choice of exponent 1+1/d in the approximation bound is precisely what gives the denominator-power q^{d+1} in the counting sum.
mathContext: For $\alpha \in [0,1]^d$, the approximation condition: $\exists$ primitive $p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ s.t. $\max_i |\alpha_i - p_i/q| < A/q^{1+1/d}$. The box volume is $(2A/q^{1+1/d})^d = (2A)^d/q^{d+1}$. Summing over primitive $p$ with denominator $q$ gives contribution $J_d(q) \cdot (2A)^d/q^{d+1}$ to the measure. The exponent $1+1/d$ is the natural 'threshold' exponent from the Jarník–Besicovitch theorem in $d$ dimensions.

title: f_d Formula: Properties and Consistency Lemmas
content: The limit formula f_d(A,c) = (2A)^d·log(c)/ζ(d+1) is defined as a Lean `noncomputable def`. Several algebraic properties are proved: positivity (for A,c > 0,1), vanishing (at A=0 or c=1), A^d-scaling, monotonicity in c, and the dimension recurrence f_{d+1}·ζ(d+2) = 2A·(f_d·ζ(d+1)). The consistency check `f_d_one_is_est` is particularly important: it verifies that f_1(A,c) = 2A·log(c)/ζ(2) = 2A·log(c)/(π²/6) = 12A·log(c)/π², matching the classical EST formula. This uses `zetaAtSucc_one` (Basel problem axiom) and `field_simp; ring`.
mathContext: The formula $f_d(A,c) = (2A)^d \cdot \frac{\log c}{\zeta(d+1)}$ encodes: $(2A)^d$ = volume of approximation box per lattice point, $\log c$ = logarithmic measure of the denominator interval $[N, cN]$ as $N \to \infty$, $1/\zeta(d+1)$ = density of primitive $d$-tuples (from Jordan-Mertens). Consistency: $f_1 = 12A\log c/\pi^2$ ✓, $f_2 = 4A^2\log c/\zeta(3)$ ✓ (Apéry's constant).

title: Jordan-Mertens and Main Theorem: The Two Core Axioms
content: The two central results are both axioms, reflecting deep analytic number theory not yet in Mathlib. The Jordan-Mertens axiom states that ζ(d+1)·Σ_{q=N}^{cN} J_d(q)/q^{d+1} → log(c) as N→∞. This is the d-dimensional analog of the classical Mertens' third theorem (Σ_{p≤N} 1/p ~ log log N). The formulation uses `Filter.Tendsto` with `Filter.atTop`, the standard Lean/Mathlib way to express N→∞ limits. The main theorem axiom directly asserts the measure convergence S_d(N,A,c) → f_d(A,c) under the EST regime condition A < 1/(2(d+1)). The docstring includes a careful note about the Dirichlet series identity Σ J_d(q)/q^s = ζ(s)/ζ(s+d), and the subtle distinction between the Dirichlet series at s and the partial sum estimate.
mathContext: Jordan-Mertens (d-dim): $\zeta(d+1) \sum_{q=N}^{\lceil cN \rceil} \frac{J_d(q)}{q^{d+1}} \to \log c$ as $N \to \infty$. This uses: (1) $\sum_{q=1}^N J_d(q) \sim N^{d+1}/(d+1)\cdot 1/\zeta(d+1)$ (partial sums of Jordan totient), (2) summation-by-parts (Abel summation). Compare with classical Mertens: $\sum_{q \leq N} \varphi(q)/q \sim 6N/\pi^2$, giving $\sum_{q=N}^{cN} \varphi(q)/q^2 \sim 6\log(c)/\pi^2$.

title: Corollaries: EST Consistency, Apéry, Dimension Curse, Recurrence
content: Six corollaries verify the formula's structure. (1) `d1_is_est`: d=1 gives exactly the EST formula 12A·log(c)/π². (2) `d2_formula`: d=2 gives f_2 = 4A²·log(c)/ζ(3), involving Apéry's constant ζ(3) ≈ 1.202 — proved by irrationality by Apéry in 1979. (3) `f_d_dimension_decay` (axiom): for A < 1/2, f_d → 0 as d → ∞, reflecting the 'dimension curse'. (4) `est_regime_d1_matches`: the d=1 EST condition A < 1/4 implies A < 1/2. (5) Numerical example: f_1(1/2, 2) = 6·log(2)/π². (6) Recurrence f_{d+1}·ζ(d+2) = 2A·f_d·ζ(d+1). All proved algebraically except the dimension decay axiom.
mathContext: Dimension curse: $(2A)^d \to 0$ as $d \to \infty$ when $A < 1/2$, since $2A < 1$. This means simultaneous approximation of $d$ irrationals becomes exponentially rare in high dimensions — a fundamental obstruction to multidimensional equidistribution. Apéry's constant $\zeta(3) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty 1/n^3 \approx 1.202$, proved irrational by Roger Apéry (1979) using rapidly converging integer sequences.
